title: Lagaan Returns to Cinemas This Thursday. Twenty-Five Years Later, It Still Makes You Believe.
excerpt: Aamir Khan's Oscar-nominated underdog epic gets a three-day theatrical re-release and a massive cast reunion that's already making people emotional.
body:
There's a moment in Lagaan — you know the one — where Bhuvan looks up at the sky and waits for rain. The entire village is behind him. The British officers are smirking. The cricket pitch is dust. And somehow, impossibly, you believe they're going to win.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Nhi4Azs2nEw

Twenty-five years after that moment first hit Indian screens, Lagaan: Once Upon a Time in India is returning to cinemas on June 12 for a limited three-day theatrical run. The film completes 25 years on June 15, and Aamir Khan Productions isn't letting the occasion pass quietly.

Back on the Big Screen

The three-day window beginning Thursday gives audiences — many of whom were children in 2001, or weren't born yet — a chance to experience Ashutosh Gowariker's epic on the big screen for the first time. In an era of ₹500-crore opening weekends and superhero franchises, there's something quietly radical about a small-village cricket drama returning to multiplexes and commanding attention.

Lagaan wasn't just a film. It was an event. It ran for 50 consecutive weeks in some theatres, became one of the few Indian films to receive an Academy Award nomination for Best Foreign Language Film, and turned A.R. Rahman's "Mitwa" and "Ghanan Ghanan" into songs that entire stadiums could sing. It won multiple National Film Awards and Filmfare Awards, and cemented Aamir Khan's reputation as the man willing to bet everything on a story nobody else would touch.

The Reunion Nobody Expected

Here's where it gets emotional. According to reports, Aamir Khan is throwing a massive reunion bash on Saturday, June 13, at a five-star hotel in Mumbai. And this isn't one of those A-list-only affairs. Every single unit member has been invited — not just the principal cast, but the crew, the technicians, the people who built that cricket pitch in the sweltering heat of Bhuj.

"Aamir Khan is quite excited to throw this bash and celebrate a film which is close to his heart. He's eagerly looking forward to meeting the team and having a gala time with them. It'll surely be an evening to remember." — Source close to the production

The guest list reads like a walk through Indian cinema history: Gracy Singh, Rachel Shelley, Paul Blackthorne, Raghubir Yadav, Yashpal Sharma, Suhasini Mulay, and dozens more. For cinephiles, the prospect of seeing this ensemble together again — many of whom went on to wildly different career paths — is the kind of event that makes you wish you had a party invitation.

The Personal Layer

Lagaan also carries a uniquely intimate history for Aamir Khan. His then-wife Reena Dutta served as executive producer on the film, overseeing the massive production that shot for months in Gujarat's punishing summer heat. His future second wife, Kiran Rao, worked on set as an assistant director — their paths crossing for the first time against the backdrop of a film about impossible odds and stubborn hope.

Now, at 61, Aamir is preparing to marry for the third time. He's currently in Los Angeles with Gauri Spratt, and the couple is set to tie the knot on July 5. A month after that, his latest production — the newly retitled Batwara 1947 starring Sunny Deol and Preity Zinta — arrives in cinemas on August 14. The man is having a year.

Why This Matters for the Diaspora

For NRIs, Lagaan occupies a specific, almost sacred space in memory. It was the film you explained to your American roommate. The one that made cricket make sense to people who had never watched a single over. The Oscar nomination felt like a collective win — not just for Bollywood, but for every Indian abroad who'd ever felt their cinema was dismissed as "just song and dance."

The re-release lands on the same day as Imtiaz Ali's Main Vaapas Aaunga, another story about partition, longing, and homecoming — scored by the same A.R. Rahman. That coincidence feels almost poetic: two films about the borders we carry inside us, sharing the same release date a quarter-century apart.

Reactions from the diaspora highlight Lagaan's enduring impact. Many NRIs recall watching the film during family gatherings, sparking conversations about identity and heritage. The film's themes resonate deeply, reminding them of their roots while navigating life abroad. For those who send remittances back home, Lagaan serves as a cultural touchstone that reinforces their connection to India, making it more than just a film — it's a bridge across continents.

The Verdict

Lagaan doesn't need a re-release to be remembered. But seeing it on the big screen — hearing the crowd roar when Bhuvan hits that six, feeling the collective intake of breath during the final over — that's something no streaming platform can replicate. If you're near a theatre showing it this week, go. Take someone who's never seen it. Watch their face during the rain scene.

Some films age. Lagaan just waits for you to come back.
